report:
### Conclusion

The claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes an increase in autism is **false and unsupported by scientific evidence**.

Extensive epidemiological studies and systematic reviews by leading health organizations—including the World Health Organization (WHO), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Mayo Clinic, and the Institute of Medicine (IOM)—have repeatedly investigated this concern. Research specifically evaluating cumulative antigen exposure from the recommended childhood immunization schedule found no link between the total number of vaccines or vaccine antigens administered to infants and the risk of developing autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

Multiple large-scale studies have also evaluated specific vaccines (such as MMR) and vaccine ingredients (such as thimerosal and aluminum adjuvants), finding no causal connection to autism. Public health agencies attribute the observed historical rise in autism diagnoses to expanded diagnostic criteria, improved screening, and heightened clinical awareness rather than vaccination schedules.

### Sources

* [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/autism-spectrum-disorders)
* [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/autism-spectrum-disorder/symptoms-causes/syc-20352928)
* [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/vaccine-safety/vaccines/mmr.html)
* [Academic Pediatrics / Institute of Medicine Report](https://www.academicpedsjnl.net/article/S1876-2859(13)00159-9/fulltext)
